chunks: Whoever worships God through imagination (mere conjecture) has committed disbelief; and whoever worships the name without the meaning has committed disbelief; and whoever worships the name and the meaning has committed shirk (polytheism).

And whoever worships the meaning by applying the names upon Him with His attributes with which He described Himself — so he pacts his heart upon it, and his tongue speaks with it in his private and public life — then those are the true companions of the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him).
And in another narration: those are the true believers.

key_terms.التَّوَهُّم: al-Tawahhum — imagination, conjecture, the faculty of forming mental images. Worshipping God through this faculty means projecting a mental image or likeness onto God, which negates His transcendence.
key_terms.الِاسْم: al-Ism — the name; in theological context, the linguistic label without its referent. Worshipping only the name means treating 'Allah' as a mere word, disconnected from the divine reality.
key_terms.الْمَعْنَى: al-Ma'na — the meaning/reality; the divine reality or essence as opposed to the linguistic label. True worship requires orienting toward the divine reality itself.
key_terms.بِإِيقَاعِ الْأَسْمَاءِ: Bi-iqa' al-asma' — by applying the names; using God's revealed names as means to access and affirm the divine reality without conflating the name with an image or making it a separate entity.
key_terms.سَرَائِر وَعَلَانِيَة: Sara'ir wa-'alaniyah — private and public; inner secret life and outward conduct. True faith must be consistent across both spheres.

ai.seo_question: What does Imam Sadiq say about the correct way to worship God and the difference between kufr, shirk, and true iman?
ai.summary: Imam Sadiq (AS) delineates four categories of worshippers in ascending order: those who worship through mere imagination (kufr), those who worship only the divine name without its meaning (kufr), those who worship both name and meaning as if they were separable entities (shirk), and the true worshippers who worship the divine reality by applying God's own self-described names and attributes — with both heart and tongue, in private and in public. This teaching addresses early theological debates about the nature of divine attributes (sifat) and how God is to be worshipped correctly, distinguishing pure tawhid from subtle forms of anthropomorphism and polytheism.
